system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 21 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis, and treated hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for worsening dyspnea due to a recurrent right pleural effusion. He also reported increasing abdominal distension from ascites. Imaging confirmed a large pleural effusion and moderate ascites, with stable findings in the liver and portal vein. He underwent a therapeutic thoracentesis, removing 3.35 liters of fluid, and a paracentesis, removing 1.1 liters, both without complications. Albumin was given post-thoracentesis. His nadolol was held due to hypotension but restarted at discharge. Warfarin was resumed at a reduced dose of 1.5 mg daily. Labs showed stable liver function, mild hyponatremia, and a rise in creatinine consistent with hepatorenal syndrome. He improved clinically, with resolution of dyspnea and edema, and was discharged home with follow-up for transplant evaluation and INR monitoring.

PROCEDURE:  1. Paracentesis.
2. Right internal jugular venous access using ultrasound.
3. Paraumbilical vein access using ultrasound.
4. Pre-procedure right atrial, and portal vein pressure measurements.
5.  Contrast enhanced portal venogram.
6. Cannulation of the left portal vein via the middle hepatic vein.
7. Ethanol sclerosis and Amplatzer plug embolization of the coronary vein
varices via the paraumbilical vein access sheath.
8. Deployment of a 10 x 6 x 2 Viatorr TIPS stent.
9. Re-measurement of right atrial, and portal vein pressure.
10. Dilation of the TIPS stent with a 6 x 40 mm Mustang balloon.
11. Measurement of right atrial and portal vein pressures.
12. Post-TIPS splenic venogram.
13. Closure of the paraumbilical vein access site with Angioseal device.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
healthcare proxy. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and
placed supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per
___ protocol. The neck and abdomen were prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.

PARACENTESIS: Under US guidance, and micropuncture needle was inserted in the
right upper quadrant next to the liver. A nitinol wire was passed through the
needle into the peritoneal cavity and the needle exchanged for a micropuncture
sheath after a skin ___. The wire was then exchanged for ___ wire and a 6
F general purpose drainage catheter was then placed in the peritoneal cavity
and connected to vacuum bottles. By the end of the procedure, 5 L of yellowish
ascitic fluid had been removed.

PARAUMBILICAL VEIN CANNULATION, VARICOUS GASTRIC CORONARY VEIN EMBOLIZATION
AND TIPS PROCEDURE:

Under continuous US guidance, access into the superficial recanalized
paraumbilical vein was obtained approximately 5 cm above the umbilicus. A
nitinol wire was advanced into the vein, and after a skin ___ the
micropuncture ecotip needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath. The wire
was then exchanged for a glidewire and the micropuncture sheath exchanged for
a Kumpe catheter. The glidewire/Kumpe catheter combo was used to advance
through the paraumbilical vein into the SMV following its trajectory through
the falciform ligament cleft in the liver. The wire was exchanged for an
Amplatz wire and the Kumpe exchanged for a ___ F 45 cm sheath which was parked
into the SMV. We then proceeded to advance a straight flush catheter into the
SMV and splenic vein respectively with the aid of a glidewire, and SMV and
splenic venograms were obtained each time after confirming catheter position
by hand injection. The results are detailed in the findings.

Next, under continuous ultrasound guidance, the patent right internal jugular
vein was compressible and accessed using a micropuncture needle. Images of
ultrasound access were stored on PACS. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed
into the right atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. A small incision was made
at the needle entry site. The needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.
The Nitinol wire was removed and an Amplatz wire was advanced distally into
the IVC.

The micropuncture sheath was then removed and a 10 ___ sheath from the
___ TIPS set was advanced over the wire into the right atrium.  The
Amplatz wire was left into the IVC for stability.  At this point portal and
right atrial pressure measurements were obtained.  Given the results of the
venograms and the pressure measurements, the decision to place a TIPS stent
was made.

A C2 Cobra catheter was advanced next to the Amplatz through the IJ sheath and
access was obtained in the right hepatic first and middle hepatic vein later
using the aid of a glide wire. Position in the desired middle hepatic vein was
confirmed in the lateral projection. The glidewire was then exchanged for a
___ wire and the sheath was advanced into the distal middle hepatic vein
(after removal of the safety Amplatz that was in place).  Once the sheath was
placed in an appropriate position, the cannula device was inserted over the
___ wire and the wire was exchanged for ___ needle. The angled
sheath was turned anteriorly. The needle was then advanced through liver
parenchyma and the needle was withdrawn over its sheath. The needle sheath was
withdrawn while gentle suction was applied.  Upon blood return, an exchange
length Glidewire was introduced into the catheter to pass into the SMV. A
straight flush catheter was advanced over the wire into the SMV. The wire was
exchanged for an exchange length Amplatz wire which was advanced into the SMV
and the sheath of the metal cannula and the TIPS sheath were advanced in a
consecutive fashion into the portal vein. Once the TIPS sheath was in the
portal vein the metal cannula and its sheath were removed and a contrast
injection was performed to confirm portal anatomy.

We then decided to embolize the varicose coronary vein.  Anatomy was more
favorable to select the coronary vein from the umbilical vein sheath.  With
the aid of a Kumpe and glidewire, we gained access into the coronary vein. The
glidewire was exchanged for ___ and the ___ F sheath was advanced
approximately 5 cm past the ostium of the coronary vein in the portal vein. A
___ balloon was then advanced though the sheath and parked distally into
the coronary vein. The balloon was inflated to prevent reflux and sclerosis of
the vein was performed with 15 cc of dehydrated ethanol after measurement of
approximate volume needed by contrast injection. We then removed the ___
balloon and proceeded to embolize the vein with a 12 mm Amplatzer 4 plug. 
Subsequent contrast injection showed distal occlusion of the coronary vein and
proximal filling of gastric varices.  Further ethanol sclerosis of the gastric
varices was performed.  A 10 mm Amplatzer 1 plug was now deployed in the
coronary vein across origin of the gastric varices. Contrast injection
confirmed appropriate position of the plugs and stoppage of flow into the
coronary vein.  A wire was passed through the sheath and parked into the ___
for security and the paraumbilical access sheath was removed and parked into
the distal paraumbilical vein before its junction with the portal vein.

Next, we proceeded to deploy a 10 mm x 6 cm x 2 cm Viatorr covered stent from
the middle hepatic vein to the left portal vein.  Following stent deployment,
we re-measured right atrial and portal vein pressures. As the portosystemic
gradient continued to be 20 mmHg, we proceeded to dilate the stent to 6 mm
with a 6 x 40 mm Mustang balloon. Pressure were obtained again which yielded a
satisfactory portosystemic gradient of 10 mmHg.

A splenic venogram was performed.  After review of the images, the straight
flush catheter was then withdrawn.

The paracentesis catheter was removed and a purse-string suture applied to
prevent ascitic fluid leaking. The sheath was then removed from the right
internal jugular vein site and pressure held for 10 minutes to achieve
hemostasis. Steri-strips and sterile dressings were applied.  The
paraumbilical vein access was closed with the use of Angioseal, after which 5
min of manual pressure were applied to achieve hemostasis.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
post-procedure complications. The patient was transferred to the MICU in
stable condition.

FINDINGS: 

1. Pre-TIPS right atrial pressure of 16 mmHg and portal vein pressure of 36
mmHg resulting in a portosystemic gradient of 20 mmHg.
2.  Pre-TIPS SMV venogram showing an attenuated right portal vein and a
dilated left portal vein with minimal flow into the liver. Most flow is
diverted to numerous collaterals through portosystemic shunts, primarily a
large coronary vein feeding esophageal and gastric body varices, smaller
gastric collaterals and the paraumbiliacal veins.
3. Pre-TIPS splenic venogram showing similar shunting pathways as the SMV
venogram described above. Of note, there is no evidence of  any prominent left
gastric venous collateral.
4. Successful ethanol and Amplatzer plug embolization of the coronary vein and
communicating gastric and esophageal varices.
5. Successful deployment of a 10 x 6 x 2 Viatorr covered TIPS stent.
Re-measurement of portosystemic gradient without dilatation of the stent
yielded a result of 20 mmHg. Hence, the stent was under-dilated to 6 mm and
re-measurement of portosystemic gradient after stent dilatation yielded a
satisfactory portosystemic gradient of 10 mmHg (right atrial 14 mmHg and
portal vein 24 mmHg).
6.  Post-TIPS splenic venogram showing appropriate flow through the TIPS
stent, no flow into the embolized coronary vein, and no evidence of any large
residual varicose veins.
7. 5 liters of yellowish ascitic fluid removed through paracentesis drain.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Ethanol and plug embolization of large esophageal and gastric varices.
2.  Intra-procedural decision to place a TIPS due to elevated portosystemic
gradient.  Successful right internal jugular access with transjugular
intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placement with decrease in porto-systemic
pressure gradient from 20 to 10 mmHg. Satisfactory angiographic result.
3. 5 liters of yellowish ascites were drained.

conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The fluid has reaccumulated quickly—just days after your last procedure. We’re concerned it might be getting harder to manage with repeated thoracenteses. We’ll need to look into why it’s coming back so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be infection? I’ve been coughing more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. We’re checking for pneumonia with a CT scan tomorrow. We also need to rule out other causes. Your liver pressures might be very high, which can cause this fluid to keep coming back.

conversation_lines.text: Infection in my belly? How did that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With advanced liver disease, bacteria can end up in the fluid around your intestines. It’s not from a bad diet or anything you did. We treat it with antibiotics, and you’ll need to stay on a low-dose one afterward to prevent it from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have concerning news. You passed black stool, and your blood count dropped. We did an endoscopy and found a bleeding varix in your stomach. It wasn’t safe to band it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bleeding? From my stomach? I didn’t feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s internal. You lost a lot of blood. We gave you 7 units of blood. Because the bleeding didn’t stop, we need to do a procedure called TIPS to reduce the pressure in your liver veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TIPS? What is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It stands for Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt. We’ll create a small tunnel in your liver to redirect blood flow and lower the pressure that’s causing the varices to bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The TIPS procedure was successful. The pressure in your liver veins dropped from 20 to 10 mmHg. The bleeding has stopped. You’ll stay in the ICU for a few days to monitor for complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I feel more confused today. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be hepatic encephalopathy—your liver isn’t clearing toxins well. We’re increasing your lactulose and adding rifaximin to help. We’ll also check for infections that could be making it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you back to the regular floor today. Your breathing is better, and the TIPS is working. No more bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to do an MRI to check your liver cancer status and a heart catheterization for your transplant evaluation. The TIPS helps, but we need to make sure you’re still a candidate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI shows one liver lesion has grown to 2 cm and now meets transplant criteria for concern. There’s another suspicious spot. The transplant team will discuss whether this affects your eligibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might not qualify anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. The team will review everything—your heart, liver, and overall condition. The heart cath showed some blockage, but your bypass grafts are open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium was low when you came in, but it’s stable now. We held your diuretics and gave you a special IV fluid. We’ll restart them slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember feeling very weak. Is that from the low sodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that can cause confusion and weakness. We’re watching it closely. Your liver makes it hard to balance your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping the IV antibiotics today. You’ve completed a 7-day course for the abdominal infection. You’ll switch to a daily pill to prevent it from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat more now? I’ve had no salt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can start low-sodium foods. We’ll adjust your diet as you improve. Your ascites is still there, but the TIPS should help reduce it over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked the TIPS with an ultrasound. It’s open and working well. The blood is flowing through it like it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my warfarin? I was on it for the blood clots in my liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it during the bleeding, but now that you’re stable, we’ll restart it at a lower dose. We’ll monitor your INR closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has improved. The pleural effusion hasn’t come back since the TIPS. That’s a good sign it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe so much better. I was scared I’d need another drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful the TIPS will keep that from happening. It reduces the pressure that causes the fluid to leak into your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your encephalopathy is improving. You’re more alert. We’ll keep you on lactulose and rifaximin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. I was so foggy for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infections and bleeding can trigger that. Now that those are under control, your brain should clear up more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall and hit your head. We did a CT scan. No bleeding or fracture. But we see changes from long-term small vessel disease, which is common with your conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even remember falling. Was I confused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll make sure your walker is here and someone checks on you at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team met. They’re still reviewing your case. The new liver lesion is a concern, but they haven’t decided yet. We’re still hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I know it’s complicated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have your MRI results. The main lesion is still concerning, but no new cancers were found. The team will discuss it again next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home with services. We’ll drain some more fluid from your belly one last time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How much fluid do you think is left?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A lot—probably around 5 to 6 liters. Removing it will help your breathing and comfort at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The heart cath showed your bypass grafts are open, but there’s some narrowing in a native artery. Your cardiologist will follow up, but it doesn’t change your current plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not worse. My heart’s been okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the paracentesis this morning. We removed 5.8 liters of fluid. You’re feeling better already, I hope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my belly feels so much lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll need close follow-up with your liver and heart doctors. Watch for fever, confusion, black stools, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything. It’s been a rough few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot—bleeding, infection, confusion—but you’ve responded well. The TIPS has made a big difference. We’ll keep working on your transplant status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just grateful to be going home. I’ll keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your warfarin will be 1.5 mg daily. We’ll check your INR in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking the ciprofloxacin, lactulose, and rifaximin. They’re important for preventing infections and encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take them every day. No skipping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Someone will help you with the walker at home. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule your transplant follow-up. They’ll decide based on the MRI and heart results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for whatever comes next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. You’ve handled this incredibly well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the transport team will take you home shortly. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you with the transplant decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be waiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and portal hypertension, was admitted with worsening dyspnea and cough due to a recurrent right pleural effusion. He developed spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, requiring antibiotic treatment, and suffered a variceal bleed that was not amenable to endoscopic banding. He underwent an emergent TIPS procedure, which successfully reduced portal pressure and stopped the bleeding. He received 7 units of packed red blood cells and was managed for hepatic encephalopathy and hyponatremia. A new 2.0 cm liver lesion meeting OPTN 5b criteria was identified on MRI, and cardiac catheterization revealed patent bypass grafts with native coronary disease. The TIPS improved his hydrothorax and ascites, and he was discharged home on medications including ciprofloxacin, lactulose, rifaximin, and reduced-dose warfarin, with plans for transplant evaluation and close follow-up.
